bibl.title: ClassyFire: automated chemical classification with a comprehensive, computable taxonomy

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the chemical vocabulary itself - whether the classes chemists use can be written down as a single computable taxonomy, and what has to be decided to do it
span.quote: Scientists have long been driven by the desire to describe, organize, classify, and compare objects using taxonomies and/or ontologies. In contrast to biology, geology, and many other scientific disciplines, the world of chemistry still lacks a standardized chemical ontology or taxonomy.

span.label: can a comprehensive, computable chemical taxonomy be built and applied automatically, reproducing what expert chemists would assign by hand
span.quote: It is important that any automated classification tool provide a result that is identical or near-identical to the outcome of manual assignments by experts. As a result, a small number of post hoc adjustments were made for certain well-known chemical categories that are commonly identified by their biochemical context.

span.label: ChemOnt, a 4825-category structure-based chemical taxonomy, and ClassyFire, which applies it automatically - and, for this project, an explicit written record of every naming and definitional decision the builders had to make
span.quote: Altogether this extensive chemical taxonomy contains a total of 4825 chemical categories of organic (4146) and inorganic (678) compounds, in addition to the root category (Chemical entities).

span.label: method
span.quote: To simplify the chemical classification process, we chose to prioritize the category corresponding to the largest or most dominant structural feature of the chemical compounds (see below). This decision was based on the observed and historical tendencies of chemists to manually classify compounds based on the size (i.e. the number of atoms) of the most dominant structural feature. Furthermore, identifying the largest feature is a technique that is easily measurable and completely objective.

span.label: a discipline whose classes are used constantly and never formalised, so that each specialism classifies the same molecules by a different criterion with no one-to-one mapping between the schemes
span.quote: Consequently, chemists from various chemistry specializations have often attempted to create domain-specific ontologies. For instance, medicinal chemists tend to classify chemicals according to their pharmaceutical activities (antihypertensive, antibacterials) [ 9 ], whereas biochemists tend to classify chemicals according to their biosynthetic origin (leukotrienes, nucleic acids, terpenoids) [ 13 ]. Unfortunately, there is no simple one-to-one mapping for these different classification schemes, most of which are limited to very small numbers of domain-specific molecules.

span.label: manual construction of a taxonomy from existing literature terms, formal definition of each category by structural pattern, mapping to ChEBI, then automated classification evaluated against a panel of seven chemistry experts
span.term: manual construction of a taxonomy from existing literature terms, formal definition of each category by structural pattern, mapping to ChEBI, then automated classification evaluated against a panel of seven chemistry experts
span.quote: The results were then manually reviewed by a panel of seven chemistry experts from three different countries (Additional file 4 : Sheet 2). A total of 21,102 category assignments were made, for an average of 26.38 assignments per compound.

span.label: **WHEN TWO NAMES COMPETE, COUNT THE PAGES.** `the frequency with which the competing terms were used was OBJECTIVELY MEASURED (using GOOGLE PAGE STATISTICS or literature count statistics). Those having the highest frequency would generally take precedence`
span.quote: In some cases multiple, equivalent terms were used to describe the same compounds or categories (imidazolines vs. dihydroimidazoles). To resolve these disputes, the frequency with which the competing terms were used was objectively measured (using Google page statistics or literature count statistics). Those having the highest frequency would generally take precedence.

span.label: **and the count is then overruled by authority.** `Imidazolines` has 229,000 hits and `Dihydroimidazoles` 4590 - and where IUPAC or an expert panel recommends the less common term, `these would TAKE PRECEDENCE OVER terms initially chosen by our initial 'popularity' selection criteria`. The losing terms become synonyms
span.quote: However, attention was also paid to the scientific community and expert panels. When available, the IUPAC term was used to name a specific category. Otherwise, if the experts clearly recommended a set of (less frequently used) terms, these would take precedence over terms initially chosen by our initial “popularity” selection criteria. Examples include the terms “Imidazolines” (229,000 Google hits) and “Dihydroimidazoles” (4590 Google hits). The other popular terms were then added as synonyms.

span.label: **A CLASS THAT CANNOT BE DEFINED IS DEFINED AS THE UNION OF ITS CHILDREN.** For lipids, phenylpropanoids, polyketides, peptidomimetics and alkaloids no SMARTS string, Markush representation or formula would serve, so `the categories were DEFINED AS A UNION OF THEIR SUBCATEGORIES that were formally expressed`
span.quote: In rare cases, some categories of compounds could not be accurately described in an explicit and formal way using any SMARTS string, Markush representation, structural pattern, physico-chemical property or chemical formula. These included certain categories of lipids and lipid-like molecules, phenylpropanoids, polyketides, peptidomimetics and alkaloids, among others. In these cases, the categories were defined as a union of their subcategories that were formally expressed.

span.label: **WHEN TWO CLASSIFICATIONS BOTH FIT, TAKE THE LARGEST FEATURE** - `we chose to prioritize the category corresponding to the LARGEST OR MOST DOMINANT STRUCTURAL FEATURE`, justified not as truth but as tractability: `easily measurable and completely objective`
span.quote: To simplify the chemical classification process, we chose to prioritize the category corresponding to the largest or most dominant structural feature of the chemical compounds (see below). This decision was based on the observed and historical tendencies of chemists to manually classify compounds based on the size (i.e. the number of atoms) of the most dominant structural feature. Furthermore, identifying the largest feature is a technique that is easily measurable and completely objective.

span.label: and where that rule contradicts chemists, the rule is patched by hand: `a small number of POST HOC ADJUSTMENTS were made for certain well-known chemical categories that are commonly identified by their BIOCHEMICAL CONTEXT`
span.quote: It is important that any automated classification tool provide a result that is identical or near-identical to the outcome of manual assignments by experts. As a result, a small number of post hoc adjustments were made for certain well-known chemical categories that are commonly identified by their biochemical context.

span.label: **AMBIGUITY IS DESIGNED IN RATHER THAN RESOLVED.** `the notion of what is MOST DESCRIPTIVE CAN VARY FROM ONE USER TO ANOTHER, and from one context to another` - so the output carries a Direct Parent and a list of Alternative Parents beside it
span.quote: However, the notion of what is most descriptive can vary from one user to another, and from one context to another. For example, a cyclic depsipeptide could be also be classified as a lactam. Because of this ambiguity, ClassyFire also displays a list of Alternative Parents (Fig. 7 ) providing a more detailed description of the chemical.

span.label: **A DISAGREEMENT WITH ANOTHER ONTOLOGY IS RECORDED AS A SCOPE, NOT SETTLED.** exact, narrow, broad - and `related synonym` for the case where none of the three applies
span.quote: For any ChemOnt term, a synonym can have the identical meaning (exact scope), a more specific meaning (narrow scope), or a less specific meaning (broad scope). In some cases, the synonym can have slightly different meaning, so that it cannot be assigned any of the three aforementioned scope categories. In this case, it is simply called a related synonym.

span.label: **The authors dispute their own error count.** Of 17 false positives in 21,102 assignments, bixin dimethyl ester is a diterpene by structure and a tetraterpene by biosynthesis, and they conclude it `is ARGUABLY NOT A MISCLASSIFICATION` - so the reported precision depends on which criterion the reader accepts
span.quote: Based on its structure, one could argue that bixin dimethyl ester should be classified as a diterpene; but based on its biology, it should be classified as a tetraterpene derivative or as an apo-carotenoid diterpenoid (CHEBI:53186). Given that ClassyFire is designed to classify compounds on a structural basis rather than a biological or biosynthetic basis, this kind of “misclassification” is completely understandable and is arguably not a misclassification.

span.label: the classifier reads IUPAC names, and some classes are not defined by structure: leukotriene derivatives `are STILL CLASSIFIED AS LEUKOTRIENES, EVEN THOUGH they might no longer have the three conjugated double bonds`. A name-based classifier cannot follow a biosynthetic class
span.quote: For instance, ClassyFire’s reliance on IUPAC names as a classification feature continues to cause some problems, particularly for compounds such as leukotrienes. This is because the classification of leukotrienes is also partly based on their biosynthetic origin. Certain, leukotriene derivatives that are oxidized or reduced at one double-bond position are still classified as leukotrienes, even though they might no longer have the three conjugated double bonds or the fourth double bond.

span.label: **a strictly structure-based taxonomy has to refuse terms the field uses** - `beta-lactam antibiotic` is structural and functional at once, and `Because ChemOnt is strictly structure-based, THESE TERMS DO NOT APPLY`
span.quote: In some cases, the term used is based on both a structural and a functional classification. An example is the term beta-lactam antibiotic (CHEBI:27933) for Oxacillin (CID 6196). Because ChemOnt is strictly structure-based, these terms do not apply.

span.label: some categories could not be formally expressed at all and were defined as the union of their children - a definition that inherits whatever its subcategories happen to contain rather than stating a criterion
span.quote: In rare cases, some categories of compounds could not be accurately described in an explicit and formal way using any SMARTS string, Markush representation, structural pattern, physico-chemical property or chemical formula. These included certain categories of lipids and lipid-like molecules, phenylpropanoids, polyketides, peptidomimetics and alkaloids, among others. In these cases, the categories were defined as a union of their subcategories that were formally expressed.

span.label: **and the authors decline the last word:** `ClassyFire is OBVIOUSLY NOT THE FINAL WORD on chemical classification or chemical taxonomies/ontologies ... we expect that this subject (and this software) WILL EVOLVE CONSIDERABLY over the coming years`
span.quote: ClassyFire is obviously not the final word on chemical classification or chemical taxonomies/ontologies. Given the size and complexity of the global chemical space along with the rapidly evolving needs of chemists and cheminformatics specialists, we expect that this subject (and this software) will evolve considerably over the coming years.

span.label: the rank names of Linnaean biological taxonomy - Kingdom, SuperClass, Class, SubClass - are carried across to name the levels of a CHEMICAL taxonomy
span.quote: Inspired by the original Linnaean biological taxonomy [ 4 ], we assigned the terms Kingdom, SuperClass, Class, and SubClass to denote the first, second, third and fourth levels of the chemical taxonomy, respectively.

span.label: manual review of every assignment by a panel of SEVEN chemistry experts from THREE different countries - 21,102 assignments, 26.38 per compound
span.note: eliminates: the circularity of judging an automated classifier by the categories it produces; the panel supplies an answer the software did not generate · outcome: held
span.quote: The results were then manually reviewed by a panel of seven chemistry experts from three different countries (Additional file 4 : Sheet 2). A total of 21,102 category assignments were made, for an average of 26.38 assignments per compound.

span.label: reproducing ChEBI's existing annotations rather than only scoring new ones
span.note: eliminates: the possibility that ClassyFire agrees with experts only where nothing was at stake; ChEBI is an independent, hand-built vocabulary · outcome: held
span.quote: Overall, ClassyFire was able to reproduce ~94% of the ChEBI annotations, but also to suggest new terms that could accurately increase the number of annotations by another 43.6%.

span.label: measuring the competing names by external frequency - Google page statistics and literature counts - instead of by the authors' preference
span.note: eliminates: the taxonomy encoding its builders' own vocabulary; the criterion is outside the project and can be checked by anyone · outcome: partial
span.quote: In some cases multiple, equivalent terms were used to describe the same compounds or categories (imidazolines vs. dihydroimidazoles). To resolve these disputes, the frequency with which the competing terms were used was objectively measured (using Google page statistics or literature count statistics). Those having the highest frequency would generally take precedence.

span.label: chemical ontology
span.quote: Scientists have long been driven by the desire to describe, organize, classify, and compare objects using taxonomies and/or ontologies. In contrast to biology, geology, and many other scientific disciplines, the world of chemistry still lacks a standardized chemical ontology or taxonomy.

span.label: Taxonomies
span.quote: Taxonomies are simplistic schemes that help in the hierarchical classification of concepts or objects [ 1 ]. They are usually limited to a specific domain and to a single relationship type connecting one node to another. Ontologies share the hierarchical structure of taxonomies. In contrast to taxonomies, however, they often have multiple relationship types and are really designed to provide a formal naming of the types, properties and interrelationships of entities or concepts in a specific discipline, domain or field of study [ 2 , 3 ].

span.label: ChemOnt
span.quote: A total of 9012 English synonyms were added to the ChemOnt terminology data set.

span.label: ClassyFire
span.quote: Overall, ClassyFire was able to reproduce ~94% of the ChEBI annotations, but also to suggest new terms that could accurately increase the number of annotations by another 43.6%.

span.label: Kingdom
span.quote: The top level (Kingdom) partitions chemicals into two disjoint categories: organic compounds versus inorganic compounds. Organic compounds are defined as chemical compounds whose structure contains one or more carbon atoms. Inorganic compounds are defined as compounds that are not organic, with the exception of a small number of “special” compounds, including, cyanide/isocyanide and their respective non-hydrocarbyl derivatives, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, carbon sulfide, and carbon disulfide.

span.label: Direct Parent
span.quote: Alternative parents are categories that describe the compound but do not have an ancestor–descendant relationship with each other or with the Direct Parent.

span.label: Alternative Parents
span.quote: However, the notion of what is most descriptive can vary from one user to another, and from one context to another. For example, a cyclic depsipeptide could be also be classified as a lactam. Because of this ambiguity, ClassyFire also displays a list of Alternative Parents

span.label: narrow synonym
span.quote: It is worth mentioning that in the case of ChEBI, due to certain philosophical discrepancies, some terms may appear to be exact synonyms for a given ChemOnt category, but actually have a different meaning. For instance, ChEBI makes a clear distinction between “carboxylic acid” and “carboxylic acid anion”, while ChemOnt does not. Therefore, the ChEBI term “carboxylic acid” is a narrow synonym of ChemOnt’s “carboxylic acids”.

span.label: related synonym
span.quote: For any ChemOnt term, a synonym can have the identical meaning (exact scope), a more specific meaning (narrow scope), or a less specific meaning (broad scope). In some cases, the synonym can have slightly different meaning, so that it cannot be assigned any of the three aforementioned scope categories. In this case, it is simply called a related synonym.

span.label: ChEBI
span.quote: A total of 6014 category mappings were created, with an average of 1.24 ChEBI synonyms per category. Each ClassyFire category has one or more mapped ChEBI terms.

span.label: MeSH
span.quote: For instance, in the PubChem database [ 19 ], only 0.12% of the >91,000,000 compounds (as of June 2016) are actually classified via the MeSH thesaurus.

span.label: is_a
span.quote: In PubChem, it is incorrectly assigned the class of beta-lactams, which are sulfur compounds. Moreover, although the latter can be either inorganic or organic, it is wrong to describe a single compound both as organic and inorganic. The transitivity of the is_a relationship is not fulfilled, which makes the class inference difficult.

span.label: IUPAC
span.quote: However, attention was also paid to the scientific community and expert panels. When available, the IUPAC term was used to name a specific category. Otherwise, if the experts clearly recommended a set of (less frequently used) terms, these would take precedence over terms initially chosen by our initial “popularity” selection criteria. Examples include the terms “Imidazolines” (229,000 Google hits) and “Dihydroimidazoles” (4590 Google hits). The other popular terms were then added as synonyms.

span.label: structural feature
span.quote: To simplify the chemical classification process, we chose to prioritize the category corresponding to the largest or most dominant structural feature of the chemical compounds (see below). This decision was based on the observed and historical tendencies of chemists to manually classify compounds based on the size (i.e. the number of atoms) of the most dominant structural feature. Furthermore, identifying the largest feature is a technique that is easily measurable and completely objective.

span.label: false positives
span.quote: In this test, a total of 17 false positives (out of 21,102 assignments) were detected. An example is the misclassification of bixin dimethyl ester (CID14413719) as an acyclic diterpene. From a structural point of view, this compound contains a chain of four consecutive isoprene units, which is characteristic of diterpenes (Fig. 9 a).

span.label: tetraterpene derivative
span.quote: Based on its structure, one could argue that bixin dimethyl ester should be classified as a diterpene; but based on its biology, it should be classified as a tetraterpene derivative or as an apo-carotenoid diterpenoid (CHEBI:53186). Given that ClassyFire is designed to classify compounds on a structural basis rather than a biological or biosynthetic basis, this kind of “misclassification” is completely understandable and is arguably not a misclassification.

span.label: leukotrienes
span.quote: For instance, ClassyFire’s reliance on IUPAC names as a classification feature continues to cause some problems, particularly for compounds such as leukotrienes. This is because the classification of leukotrienes is also partly based on their biosynthetic origin. Certain, leukotriene derivatives that are oxidized or reduced at one double-bond position are still classified as leukotrienes, even though they might no longer have the three conjugated double bonds or the fourth double bond.

span.label: domain-specific ontologies
span.quote: Consequently, chemists from various chemistry specializations have often attempted to create domain-specific ontologies. For instance, medicinal chemists tend to classify chemicals according to their pharmaceutical activities (antihypertensive, antibacterials) [ 9 ], whereas biochemists tend to classify chemicals according to their biosynthetic origin (leukotrienes, nucleic acids, terpenoids) [ 13 ]. Unfortunately, there is no simple one-to-one mapping for these different classification schemes, most of which are limited to very small numbers of domain-specific molecules.

span.label: `taxonomy` - a hierarchical scheme limited to one domain and ONE relationship type, as this paper uses it against `ontology`
span.quote: Taxonomies are simplistic schemes that help in the hierarchical classification of concepts or objects [ 1 ]. They are usually limited to a specific domain and to a single relationship type connecting one node to another. Ontologies share the hierarchical structure of taxonomies. In contrast to taxonomies, however, they often have multiple relationship types and are really designed to provide a formal naming of the types, properties and interrelationships of entities or concepts in a specific discipline, domain or field of study [ 2 , 3 ].

span.label: `synonym` - in ChemOnt a scoped relation, not an equality: exact, narrow, broad, or related when none of the three fits
span.quote: For any ChemOnt term, a synonym can have the identical meaning (exact scope), a more specific meaning (narrow scope), or a less specific meaning (broad scope). In some cases, the synonym can have slightly different meaning, so that it cannot be assigned any of the three aforementioned scope categories. In this case, it is simply called a related synonym.

span.label: `Direct Parent` - the single most descriptive category; `most descriptive` is explicitly acknowledged to vary by user and context
span.quote: However, the notion of what is most descriptive can vary from one user to another, and from one context to another. For example, a cyclic depsipeptide could be also be classified as a lactam. Because of this ambiguity, ClassyFire also displays a list of Alternative Parents (Fig. 7 ) providing a more detailed description of the chemical.

span.label: `organic` - in ChemOnt, containing one or more carbon atoms, with a short enumerated exception list rather than a principle
span.quote: The top level (Kingdom) partitions chemicals into two disjoint categories: organic compounds versus inorganic compounds. Organic compounds are defined as chemical compounds whose structure contains one or more carbon atoms. Inorganic compounds are defined as compounds that are not organic, with the exception of a small number of “special” compounds, including, cyanide/isocyanide and their respective non-hydrocarbyl derivatives, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, carbon sulfide, and carbon disulfide.

span.label: `misclassification` - contested in this paper: an assignment the expert panel rejects may still be correct under the criterion the classifier declares
span.quote: Based on its structure, one could argue that bixin dimethyl ester should be classified as a diterpene; but based on its biology, it should be classified as a tetraterpene derivative or as an apo-carotenoid diterpenoid (CHEBI:53186). Given that ClassyFire is designed to classify compounds on a structural basis rather than a biological or biosynthetic basis, this kind of “misclassification” is completely understandable and is arguably not a misclassification.

span.label: critiques → the existing chemical classification schemes - manual, proprietary or closed-source, limited in scope, and often without meaningful names or definitions
span.quote: Overall, it should be clear that while many attempts have been made to create chemical taxonomies or ontologies, many are proprietary or “closed source”, most require manual analysis or annotation, most are limited in scope and many do not provide meaningful names, definitions or descriptors.

span.label: critiques → PubChem's class assignments, where the transitivity of is_a is broken and a single compound is described as both organic and inorganic
span.quote: In PubChem, it is incorrectly assigned the class of beta-lactams, which are sulfur compounds. Moreover, although the latter can be either inorganic or organic, it is wrong to describe a single compound both as organic and inorganic. The transitivity of the is_a relationship is not fulfilled, which makes the class inference difficult.

span.label: extends → ChEBI, whose annotations ClassyFire reproduces at ~94% and to which it proposes a further 43.6%
span.quote: Overall, ClassyFire was able to reproduce ~94% of the ChEBI annotations, but also to suggest new terms that could accurately increase the number of annotations by another 43.6%.

span.label: concedes → the classes that resist structural definition - lipids, phenylpropanoids, polyketides, peptidomimetics and alkaloids, defined here as unions of children
span.quote: In rare cases, some categories of compounds could not be accurately described in an explicit and formal way using any SMARTS string, Markush representation, structural pattern, physico-chemical property or chemical formula. These included certain categories of lipids and lipid-like molecules, phenylpropanoids, polyketides, peptidomimetics and alkaloids, among others. In these cases, the categories were defined as a union of their subcategories that were formally expressed.

Given that ClassyFire is designed to classify compounds on a structural basis rather than a biological or biosynthetic basis, this kind of “misclassification” is completely understandable and is arguably not a misclassification.

span.label: **THE TAXONOMY IS A TREE AND THE WORLD IS NOT** - ChemOnt allows one parent per node; ChEBI allows several. The shape of the vocabulary is a claim about chemistry before any term in it is
span.term: **THE TAXONOMY IS A TREE AND THE WORLD IS NOT** - ChemOnt allows one parent per node; ChEBI allows several. The shape of the vocabulary is a claim about chemistry before any term in it is
span.quote: Additionally, the two hierarchies are built differently. While ChemOnt is built as a tree, where each node has no more than one parent, a ChEBI term can have several parents.

span.label: taxonomy vs ontology - a taxonomy is hierarchical with ONE relationship type; an ontology has multiple relationship types and formally names types, properties and interrelationships
span.term: taxonomy vs ontology - a taxonomy is hierarchical with ONE relationship type; an ontology has multiple relationship types and formally names types, properties and interrelationships
span.quote: Taxonomies are simplistic schemes that help in the hierarchical classification of concepts or objects [ 1 ]. They are usually limited to a specific domain and to a single relationship type connecting one node to another. Ontologies share the hierarchical structure of taxonomies. In contrast to taxonomies, however, they often have multiple relationship types and are really designed to provide a formal naming of the types, properties and interrelationships of entities or concepts in a specific discipline, domain or field of study [ 2 , 3 ].

span.label: organic vs inorganic - organic is `chemical compounds whose structure contains one or more carbon atoms`; inorganic is `compounds that are NOT ORGANIC, WITH THE EXCEPTION OF` an enumerated list including cyanide, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and carbon disulfide
span.term: organic vs inorganic - organic is `chemical compounds whose structure contains one or more carbon atoms`; inorganic is `compounds that are NOT ORGANIC, WITH THE EXCEPTION OF` an enumerated list including cyanide, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and carbon disulfide
span.quote: The top level (Kingdom) partitions chemicals into two disjoint categories: organic compounds versus inorganic compounds. Organic compounds are defined as chemical compounds whose structure contains one or more carbon atoms. Inorganic compounds are defined as compounds that are not organic, with the exception of a small number of “special” compounds, including, cyanide/isocyanide and their respective non-hydrocarbyl derivatives, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, carbon sulfide, and carbon disulfide.

span.label: synonym scope - exact (identical meaning), narrow (more specific), broad (less specific), and related where none of the three applies
span.term: synonym scope - exact (identical meaning), narrow (more specific), broad (less specific), and related where none of the three applies
span.quote: For any ChemOnt term, a synonym can have the identical meaning (exact scope), a more specific meaning (narrow scope), or a less specific meaning (broad scope). In some cases, the synonym can have slightly different meaning, so that it cannot be assigned any of the three aforementioned scope categories. In this case, it is simply called a related synonym.

span.label: Alternative Parents - `categories that describe the compound but DO NOT HAVE AN ANCESTOR-DESCENDANT RELATIONSHIP with each other or with the Direct Parent`
span.term: Alternative Parents - `categories that describe the compound but DO NOT HAVE AN ANCESTOR-DESCENDANT RELATIONSHIP with each other or with the Direct Parent`
span.quote: Alternative parents are categories that describe the compound but do not have an ancestor–descendant relationship with each other or with the Direct Parent.

span.label: categories in ChemOnt
span.quote: Altogether this extensive chemical taxonomy contains a total of 4825 chemical categories of organic (4146) and inorganic (678) compounds, in addition to the root category (Chemical entities).

span.label: English synonyms in ChemOnt
span.quote: A total of 9012 English synonyms were added to the ChemOnt terminology data set.

span.label: ChEBI category mappings
span.quote: A total of 6014 category mappings were created, with an average of 1.24 ChEBI synonyms per category. Each ClassyFire category has one or more mapped ChEBI terms.

span.label: expert panel assignments reviewed
span.quote: The results were then manually reviewed by a panel of seven chemistry experts from three different countries (Additional file 4 : Sheet 2). A total of 21,102 category assignments were made, for an average of 26.38 assignments per compound.

span.quote: In this test, a total of 17 false positives (out of 21,102 assignments) were detected. An example is the misclassification of bixin dimethyl ester (CID14413719) as an acyclic diterpene. From a structural point of view, this compound contains a chain of four consecutive isoprene units, which is characteristic of diterpenes (Fig. 9 a).

span.quote: However, attention was also paid to the scientific community and expert panels. When available, the IUPAC term was used to name a specific category. Otherwise, if the experts clearly recommended a set of (less frequently used) terms, these would take precedence over terms initially chosen by our initial “popularity” selection criteria. Examples include the terms “Imidazolines” (229,000 Google hits) and “Dihydroimidazoles” (4590 Google hits). The other popular terms were then added as synonyms.

span.label: the largest or most dominant structural feature - the tie-breaker when two categories both fit, chosen for being `easily measurable and completely objective`
span.term: the largest or most dominant structural feature - the tie-breaker when two categories both fit, chosen for being `easily measurable and completely objective`
span.quote: To simplify the chemical classification process, we chose to prioritize the category corresponding to the largest or most dominant structural feature of the chemical compounds (see below). This decision was based on the observed and historical tendencies of chemists to manually classify compounds based on the size (i.e. the number of atoms) of the most dominant structural feature. Furthermore, identifying the largest feature is a technique that is easily measurable and completely objective.

span.label: term frequency in the literature and on the web - the variable that decides which of two competing names becomes the category
span.term: term frequency in the literature and on the web - the variable that decides which of two competing names becomes the category
span.quote: In some cases multiple, equivalent terms were used to describe the same compounds or categories (imidazolines vs. dihydroimidazoles). To resolve these disputes, the frequency with which the competing terms were used was objectively measured (using Google page statistics or literature count statistics). Those having the highest frequency would generally take precedence.
